title: Hypertension and postural hypotension
blurb: Measure blood pressure accurately, confirm hypertension with ABPM or HBPM, know the targets and drug steps, and test for postural hypotension.
question: Mrs Mensah, 82, takes amlodipine and has had two falls. Lying, her BP is 148/84 mmHg; after standing for 1 minute it is 122/76 mmHg and she feels dizzy. What does this show, and what should the nurse do next?

teach.h: Hypertension is diagnosed outside the clinic
teach.body: Formally: hypertension is confirmed when clinic BP is 140/90 mmHg or higher AND the daytime ABPM or HBPM average is 135/85 mmHg or higher (NICE NG136, updated February 2026). In plain English: one high reading in clinic is not a diagnosis. Because of the white-coat effect, the reading is confirmed with a day of ambulatory monitoring (or home readings). Home and ambulatory thresholds are 5 mmHg lower than clinic thresholds.

items: Palpate the radial or brachial pulse first: automated devices may be inaccurate if the pulse is irregular (e.g. AF). If irregular, measure manually by auscultation.
Use a validated, maintained device and the correct cuff size for the arm.
Person seated, quiet, relaxed, arm outstretched and supported, in a temperate room.
When diagnosing, measure both arms; if they differ by more than 15 mmHg on repeat, use the higher arm.
If clinic BP is 140/90 or higher, take a second reading (and a third if very different) and record the lower of the last two.

head: Stage
Clinic BP
ABPM / HBPM average
teach.caption: ABPM: at least 2 readings an hour while awake, average of at least 14. HBPM: 2 readings 1 minute apart, twice daily, for at least 4 (ideally 7) days, discarding day 1.
Step 2: add a CCB or thiazide-like diuretic to an ACEi/ARB, or an ACEi/ARB or thiazide-like diuretic to a CCB. Step 3: ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic. Never combine an ACEi with an ARB.
NG136 1.4.20–1.4.22; same targets with or without cardiovascular disease (1.4.23). Use clinical judgement in frailty or multimorbidity.

teach.body: In anyone with falls or postural dizziness, measure BP lying on their back (or seated if lying is inconvenient), then again after standing for at least 1 minute. A fall in systolic of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic of 10 mmHg or more, is significant: consider causes including medicines, manage falls risk, and measure subsequent BPs standing. Also check for postural hypotension in people with hypertension who have type 2 diabetes or are 80 or over.

steps.label: Look for red flags
steps.sub: retinal haemorrhage, papilloedema, new confusion, chest pain, heart failure, AKI

teach.caption: NG136 1.5.1–1.5.3. Suspected phaeochromocytoma (labile BP, headache, palpitations, pallor, sweating) also needs same-day referral.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Mensah in a falls clinic
teach.body: Mrs Mensah's systolic BP fell by 26 mmHg (148 to 122) after standing for 1 minute and she was dizzy: significant postural hypotension. Nurse Ellen documents both readings with positions and timings, reports the result and requests a medication review (her amlodipine may contribute). She records future BPs standing, as NG136 advises, and refers her for a falls assessment. Her BP target, at 82, is below 150/90 clinic, guided by standing readings.

teach.text: Don't mix up the two thresholds: 140/90 is the CLINIC threshold, 135/85 the home/ambulatory threshold. And for postural hypotension the drop is 20 SYSTOLIC or 10 DIASTOLIC after at least 1 minute standing, not 10 systolic. Potassium-containing salt substitutes are unsuitable for older people, people with diabetes or kidney disease and those on ACEi/ARBs.

items.label: severe: look for same-day red flags

items: Feel the pulse first; irregular pulse means a manual BP. Use the right cuff, arm supported.
Clinic 140/90+ is confirmed by ABPM or HBPM 135/85+.
Step 1: ACEi/ARB if T2DM or under 55 (not Black African/Caribbean); otherwise CCB.
Targets: below 140/90 under 80; below 150/90 at 80+. Never ACEi plus ARB.
Postural hypotension: lying then 1 minute standing; drop of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic.

summary: You can now measure BP accurately, explain how hypertension is confirmed and staged, and apply NG136 drug steps and targets. You can also test for postural hypotension correctly and recognise severe hypertension needing same-day referral.

A.q: A man's clinic BP is 152/94 mmHg on two readings. What is the next step to confirm a diagnosis of hypertension?
options: Start amlodipine and recheck in 4 weeks
A.why: NG136 1.2.3: if clinic BP is between 140/90 and 180/120, offer ABPM (or HBPM if ABPM is unsuitable) to confirm the diagnosis.

whyNot.0: Treatment usually follows confirmation, not a single clinic reading.
whyNot.1: 5-yearly checks apply when hypertension is not diagnosed.
whyNot.3: Same-day referral is for 180/120 or higher with red flags.

A.q: What ABPM daytime average confirms hypertension in someone with a clinic BP of 140/90 or higher?
A.why: NG136 1.2.8: confirm hypertension with an ABPM daytime or HBPM average of 135/85 mmHg or higher.

whyNot.0: 130/80 is below the NG136 diagnostic threshold.
whyNot.2: 140/90 is the clinic threshold; ABPM is 5 mmHg lower.
whyNot.3: 145/95 is higher than the diagnostic threshold.

A.q: A 62-year-old white British man without diabetes has confirmed stage 2 hypertension. Which step 1 drug does NG136 recommend?
A.why: NG136 1.4.35: offer a CCB to adults aged 55 or over without type 2 diabetes.

whyNot.1: ACEi/ARB is for under-55s (not Black African/Caribbean) or people with type 2 diabetes.
whyNot.2: Beta-blockers are not step 1 treatment for hypertension.
whyNot.3: A thiazide-like diuretic is used if a CCB is not tolerated or there is heart failure.

B.q: How should a nurse test for postural hypotension in a woman with dizziness on standing?
B.why: NG136 1.1.5: measure BP lying (or seated if lying is inconvenient), then after the person has been standing for at least 1 minute.

whyNot.0: 10 seconds of standing is too short.
whyNot.1: The sequence starts lying, then standing.
whyNot.2: The second reading is taken standing, not sitting.

B.q: Which result confirms significant postural hypotension under NG136?
B.why: NG136 1.1.6: a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more (here 22) or a diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more after standing for at least 1 minute.

whyNot.0: A 12 mmHg systolic fall is below the threshold.
whyNot.1: A 6 mmHg diastolic fall is below the threshold.
whyNot.3: Heart rate change is not the NG136 criterion.

B.q: A woman on ramipril for hypertension develops a persistent dry cough. What does NG136 recommend?
options: Add an ARB to the ramipril
B.why: NG136 1.4.33: if an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated (for example because of cough), offer an ARB. Do not combine an ACEi with an ARB (1.4.34).

whyNot.0: Combining an ACEi and an ARB is not recommended.
whyNot.1: Beta-blockers are not the replacement for an ACEi.
whyNot.2: Stopping all treatment leaves hypertension uncontrolled.

C.q: Mr Novak, 58, has a clinic BP of 196/124 mmHg. He reports new chest pain and is slightly confused. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange ABPM to confirm the reading
Recheck BP in clinic next week
Start a CCB and review in a month
C.why: NG136 1.5.2: refer for same-day specialist assessment if clinic BP is 180/120 or higher with life-threatening symptoms such as new confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure or AKI.

whyNot.0: ABPM delays care when life-threatening symptoms are present.
whyNot.2: A week's delay is unsafe with these symptoms.
whyNot.3: Routine outpatient treatment is inappropriate with red flags.

C.q: A nurse is about to check BP with an automated device in Mrs Clarke, 76. Her radial pulse is irregularly irregular. What should she do?
options: Use the automated device on both arms
Measure manually over the brachial artery
Take three automated readings and average
Use a larger cuff on the automated device
C.why: NG136 1.1.2: automated devices may not be accurate with pulse irregularity such as AF; measure BP manually using direct auscultation over the brachial artery.

whyNot.0: Both-arm measurement does not fix device inaccuracy in AF.
whyNot.2: Averaging inaccurate readings is still inaccurate.
whyNot.3: Cuff size should match the arm; it does not correct for an irregular pulse.

C.q: Mr Ali, 66, of Black African family origin, has type 2 diabetes and newly confirmed hypertension. Which step 1 drug is most appropriate?
C.why: NG136 1.4.32: offer an ACEi or ARB to people with type 2 diabetes of any age or family origin; 1.4.30 advises considering an ARB in preference to an ACEi for people of Black African or African–Caribbean family origin.

whyNot.0: CCB first-line applies to Black African/Caribbean adults without type 2 diabetes.
whyNot.1: A thiazide-like diuretic is not step 1 here.
whyNot.3: Alpha-blockers are a step 4 option in resistant hypertension.

reteach.title: Three readings tell three stories
reteach.question: Why does the same person have a clinic reading, a home reading and a standing reading?

blocks.body: The clinic reading is often higher because of nerves (white-coat effect), so a diagnosis needs home or ambulatory readings, which have a lower threshold (135/85 instead of 140/90). The standing reading answers a different question: does BP drop too far when the person stands, making them dizzy and likely to fall? An older person can have high BP lying and postural hypotension at the same time, so standing readings guide their treatment.

blocks.text: An 80-year-old's target is below 150/90 clinic, not 140/90. And with a postural drop, treat to the standing BP.

explain.body: Feel the pulse; if irregular, measure manually. Validated device, correct cuff, seated, arm supported. Both arms at diagnosis; use the higher arm if the difference stays above 15 mmHg.

test.q: The BP differs by 20 mmHg between a man's arms on two occasions. Which arm should be used for future readings?
options: The arm with the higher reading
The arm giving the lower reading
test.why: NG136 1.2.1: if the difference remains more than 15 mmHg on repeat, measure subsequent BPs in the arm with the higher reading.

whyNot.1: Using the lower arm would under-estimate BP.
whyNot.2: Dominance is not the deciding factor.

explain.body: Clinic 140/90+, confirm with ABPM or HBPM 135/85+. Stage 2 is clinic 160/100+ (ABPM 150/95+). Severe is clinic 180/120+.

test.q: For HBPM to confirm a diagnosis, how long should readings continue?
options: At least 14 days in a row
test.why: NG136 1.2.7: record twice daily for at least 4 days, ideally 7, discarding the first day and averaging the rest.

whyNot.0: One day is not enough for HBPM.

explain.body: Step 1: ACEi/ARB (T2DM or under 55 not Black African/Caribbean) or CCB (55+ or Black African/Caribbean without T2DM). Step 2: add one more. Step 3: ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic. Check adherence before each step.

test.q: A woman's BP is not controlled on amlodipine. What does NG136 advise the nurse to discuss before step 2?
options: Whether she takes it as prescribed
Whether she adds salt to her food
Whether she would like a beta-blocker
Whether she has had a recent ECG
test.why: NG136 1.4.40: before considering next-step treatment, discuss whether the person is taking their medicine as prescribed and support adherence.

whyNot.1: Salt reduction is advised, but adherence is the specific pre-step check.
whyNot.2: Beta-blockers are not a step 2 option.
whyNot.3: An ECG is not the NG136 pre-step requirement.

explain.body: Under 80: clinic below 140/90 (ABPM/HBPM below 135/85). 80 and over: clinic below 150/90 (below 145/85). With postural hypotension, use standing BP. Annual review for everyone with hypertension.

test.q: What is the clinic BP target for a man aged 84 with hypertension?
test.why: NG136 1.4.21: for adults aged 80 and over, reduce clinic BP to below 150/90 mmHg.

whyNot.0: 130/80 is not the NG136 target for this age.
whyNot.3: 160/100 is the stage 2 threshold, not a target.
